wowFacts: The star at its center is dying — this is its outer atmosphere, cast into space.
Over the next tens of thousands of years, this cloud will fade away.

objects.visualHint: Look for a soft apple-core glow — gas shed by a dying star, not a sharp edge.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: The light in this image began its journey around the early Middle Ages and is arriving at the telescope tonight. What made that journey is a stretched shell of gas, shed by a star in the final act of its life — its dumbbell shape comes from that shell seen from our particular angle.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: This is one of the clearest nearby examples of what our own Sun will eventually become — a preview of stellar death, several billion years early.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: First catalogued by Charles Messier in 1764 — the very first planetary nebula anyone ever recorded. He was hunting comets and kept finding things that weren't; this list of "not comets" became the Messier catalog astronomers still use tonight.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Small and dim to the naked eye, but unmistakable through a telescope — a soft, glowing patch with a faint greenish tint in dark skies.

objects.description: A dense swarm of hundreds of thousands of ancient stars packed into a shimmering ball.
Our nearest large galactic neighbor, a whole other galaxy of a trillion stars you can see with your own eyes.
wowFacts: It contains roughly a trillion stars — about four times as many as our own Milky Way.
It's the most distant thing most people will ever see with the naked eye.
Andromeda and the Milky Way may merge billions of years from now, though the exact outcome is still being studied.
What looks like a small smudge is, edge to edge, over six times wider than the full Moon.
objects.visualHint: It's bigger than it looks — the faint haze extends well past what first catches your eye.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: The light in this image began its journey roughly 2.5 million years ago — long before modern humans existed anywhere on Earth — and is arriving at the telescope tonight. What made that journey is an entire separate galaxy, seen at a steep angle: a bright core surrounded by a much fainter, sprawling disk of stars and dust.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Andromeda is the benchmark for understanding our own galaxy from the outside — we can never photograph the Milky Way's full shape from within it, but Andromeda shows us roughly what it would look like.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Recorded as a "little cloud" by Persian astronomer Al-Sufi in 964 AD, nearly a thousand years before telescopes existed to explain what it actually was.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Under dark skies, visible to the naked eye as a faint smudge — one of the few galaxies you can see without any equipment at all.

wowFacts: Its rings are countless icy pieces, mostly dust-to-boulder sized.
Saturn's average density is lower than water, which is why people say it could "float."
In places, the rings may be only tens of meters thick.
A day on Saturn lasts just over 10 hours, despite the planet being about 9× Earth's width.
objects.visualHint: Steady the view and look closely — the rings appear as a thin line or oval around a small, bright disk.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: The light in this image left Saturn about 80 minutes ago and is arriving at the telescope tonight. What made that short journey is a small golden disk with a ring system tilted at whatever angle Saturn currently presents to Earth — sometimes wide open, sometimes nearly edge-on.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Saturn is the farthest planet most people will ever see rings on directly — a genuinely rare, unmistakable sight through even a modest telescope.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Galileo first saw Saturn's rings in 1610 but couldn't explain them — his telescope was too weak to resolve the shape, and he described them as "ears" on the planet.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Look for a steady, non-twinkling point of golden light — planets don't twinkle the way stars do, which is often the easiest way to pick one out.
